quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Definitions of budgets, standards, static and flexible budgets, and favourable and unfavourable variances.

questions.q: According to the lecture, a budget is best described as:
options: A record of last year's actual spending
A quantitative expression, for a set period, of a proposed future plan of action
A list of the company's fixed costs
The difference between actual and planned results
questions.explain: A budget looks forward: it expresses a plan in numbers for a set time period. The difference between actual and plan is a variance, not a budget.

questions.q: What is a variance?
options: The budgeted amount per unit
A carefully predetermined cost
The difference between an actual result and a budgeted amount
The change in output from one month to the next
questions.explain: A variance compares actual with budget. A carefully predetermined amount, usually per unit, is a standard.

questions.q: A static budget is prepared for one level of output and is not altered after it is set, even if actual output differs.
questions.explain: That is the definition in the lecture; Webb's static budget stayed at 12,000 jackets although only 10,000 were sold. The flexible budget is the one adjusted to actual output.

questions.q: A flexible budget is:
options: A budget revised every week by the finance manager
The static budget adjusted to the actual level of output
A budget with no fixed costs
The actual results restated at budgeted prices and budgeted volume
questions.explain: The flexible budget keeps the budgeted price and unit costs but uses the actual quantity (10,000 jackets), so managers can compute a richer set of variances.

questions.q: A variance is called favourable (F) when it:
options: Is larger than Rs 100,000
Increases operating income relative to budget
Arises from selling more units
Relates to revenue rather than cost
questions.explain: F and U are defined by their effect on operating income: lower cost than budget is F, higher revenue than budget is F. A cost variance can be favourable too.

questions.q: Which step is NOT part of the budgeting cycle described in the lecture?
options: Planning the performance of the organisation and its sub-units
Providing a frame of reference against which actual results are compared
Replacing the budget with actual results at the end of the period
Investigating variations from plan and taking corrective action
questions.explain: The cycle is plan, compare, investigate and act, then plan again using the feedback. The budget is never simply replaced by actuals — it is compared with them.

questions.q: What does the master budget do?
options: Coordinates all the individual budgets — operating decisions on using resources and financing decisions on paying for them
Records only the cash budget
Shows the variance of each department
Sets the standard cost of each product
questions.explain: The master budget pulls the operating and financing budgets of all sub-units into one coordinated plan.

questions.q: A standard is a carefully predetermined amount, usually expressed per unit of output.
questions.explain: Webb's standards are Rs 180 price, Rs 99 variable cost per jacket and so on; they build the budget and are the yardstick for variances.

questions.q: The Level 0 analysis in the lecture reports which single figure?
options: The flexible-budget variance of revenue
The sales-volume variance
The static-budget variance of operating income
The variance of each cost line
questions.explain: Level 0 is the one-line comparison of actual operating income with the static budget: 25,000 − 262,000 = 237,000 U. Levels 1 and 2 break it down.

questions.q: Which variance does the lecture say operating managers can 'really be held to'?
options: The static-budget variance
The sales-volume variance
The flexible-budget variance
The Level 0 variance
questions.explain: The flexible-budget variance compares actual results with the budget for the output actually achieved, removing the effect of selling fewer units, which is the sales-volume variance.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The formulas behind each column of the Webb sheet and how the variances relate to one another.

questions.q: Flexible-budget revenue is calculated as:
options: Actual price × actual quantity
Budgeted price × budgeted quantity
Budgeted price × actual quantity
Actual price × budgeted quantity
questions.explain: 180 × 10,000 = Rs 1,800,000. Budgeted price × budgeted quantity (Rs 2,160,000) is the static budget, and actual price × actual quantity is the actual result.

questions.q: Flexible-budget total cost equals:
options: Budgeted unit variable cost × actual quantity + budgeted fixed cost
Budgeted unit variable cost × budgeted quantity + budgeted fixed cost
Actual variable cost + actual fixed cost
Budgeted fixed cost × actual quantity
questions.explain: Variable cost flexes with output (99 × 10,000 = 990,000) while fixed cost stays at the budgeted Rs 710,000. Fixed cost is never multiplied by quantity.

questions.q: The static-budget variance equals which sum?
options: Flexible-budget variance − sales-volume variance
Flexible-budget variance + sales-volume variance
Price variance + efficiency variance
Actual results + static budget
questions.explain: 237,000 U = 75,000 U (flexible-budget) + 162,000 U (sales-volume). The split is the whole point of Level 2 analysis.

questions.q: The sales-volume variance for operating income can be found as:
options: (Actual units − static-budget units) × budgeted selling price
(Actual units − static-budget units) × budgeted contribution margin per unit
(Actual price − budgeted price) × actual units
Actual contribution margin − flexible-budget contribution margin
questions.explain: (10,000 − 12,000) × (180 − 99) = −2,000 × 81 = 162,000 U. Using the price alone gives the revenue part only (360,000 U), ignoring the variable cost saved.

questions.q: The sales-volume variance for fixed costs is always zero when the actual fixed cost equals budget.
questions.explain: The sales-volume variance of fixed cost is zero because budgeted fixed cost is the same in the static and flexible budgets, regardless of volume. Any difference between actual and budgeted fixed cost appears in the flexible-budget variance (5,000 F for Webb).

questions.q: If actual units sold had equalled the static-budget units, which variance would be zero?
options: The flexible-budget variance
The sales-volume variance
The static-budget variance
The fixed-cost variance
questions.explain: With no difference in volume, the flexible budget equals the static budget and the sales-volume variance disappears; the static-budget variance would then equal the flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: Webb's actual revenue is Rs 1,850,000 on 10,000 jackets against a budgeted price of Rs 180. The revenue flexible-budget variance of 50,000 F tells us that:
options: Webb sold more jackets than planned
The average selling price was Rs 5 above budget
Variable costs were lower than planned
The static budget was wrong
questions.explain: 1,850,000 ÷ 10,000 = Rs 185 per jacket, Rs 5 above the budgeted Rs 180; 5 × 10,000 = 50,000 F. Volume effects are in the sales-volume variance, not here.

questions.q: Which column of the Level 2 sheet is identical for revenue, variable cost and contribution margin in BOTH the flexible and static budgets per unit?
options: Actual price and actual unit cost
Budgeted price and budgeted unit variable cost
Actual units
Flexible-budget variances
questions.explain: Both budgets use the same Rs 180 price and Rs 99 unit variable cost; they differ only in the quantity (10,000 vs 12,000).

questions.q: In the lecture's sign convention, a positive variance is favourable and a negative one (shown in brackets) is unfavourable.
questions.explain: The sheets state 'positive = F, negative = U'; so revenue 50,000 is F and variable costs (130,000) is U. Note that lecture 14 uses the opposite sign for its cost variances.

questions.q: Budgeted contribution margin per jacket is Rs 81. If budgeted variable cost rises to Rs 105 with the price unchanged, the sales-volume variance for the same 2,000-unit shortfall would:
options: Rise to 210,000 U
Fall to 150,000 U
Stay at 162,000 U
Become favourable
questions.explain: Contribution falls to 180 − 105 = Rs 75; 2,000 × 75 = 150,000 U. The lower the margin per unit, the less a volume shortfall hurts operating income.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Rebuild the Webb Company sheet line by line and try a few variations.

questions.q: Webb budgeted 12,000 jackets at Rs 180 with variable cost Rs 99 per jacket and fixed costs of Rs 710,000. What is the static-budget operating income?
questions.explain: Contribution 12,000 × 81 = Rs 972,000; less fixed Rs 710,000 = Rs 262,000.

questions.q: Using the same budget (price Rs 180, variable cost Rs 99, fixed Rs 710,000), what is the flexible-budget operating income for 10,000 jackets?
questions.explain: 10,000 × 81 = Rs 810,000 contribution less Rs 710,000 fixed = Rs 100,000.

questions.q: Actual results: revenue Rs 1,850,000, variable costs Rs 1,120,000, fixed costs Rs 705,000. What is actual operating income?
Actual operating income is Rs 25,000 and the static budget is Rs 262,000. What is the static-budget variance (Level 0)? Give an unfavourable variance as a negative number.
Budgeted contribution margin is Rs 81 per jacket; 10,000 were sold against a static budget of 12,000. What is the sales-volume variance of operating income? (Unfavourable as a negative number.)
questions.explain: −2,000 × 81 = −162,000, i.e. 162,000 U — the whole effect of the volume shortfall, including the variable cost saved.

questions.q: Actual variable costs were Rs 1,120,000 on 10,000 jackets; the budgeted unit variable cost is Rs 99. What is the flexible-budget variance for variable costs? (Unfavourable as a negative number.)
questions.explain: Flexible budget = 99 × 10,000 = Rs 990,000; actual Rs 1,120,000 is Rs 130,000 higher, so 130,000 U. Actual unit variable cost was Rs 112.

questions.q: Actual revenue was Rs 1,850,000 for 10,000 jackets and the static budget was 12,000 jackets at Rs 180. What is the Level 1 static-budget variance for revenue? (Unfavourable as a negative number.)
questions.explain: 1,850,000 − 2,160,000 = −310,000 (310,000 U). Level 2 shows this is 50,000 F price effect and 360,000 U volume effect.

questions.q: Webb's budgeted variable cost per jacket is made of materials 60, manufacturing labour 16, variable manufacturing overhead 12, direct marketing labour 6 and variable marketing overhead 5. What is the budgeted variable marketing cost (labour plus overhead) for 10,000 jackets?
questions.explain: Marketing labour 6 + marketing overhead 5 = Rs 11 per jacket; × 10,000 = Rs 110,000. The manufacturing part is 88 × 10,000 = Rs 880,000.

questions.q: Actual fixed costs were Rs 705,000 against a budget of Rs 710,000. The fixed-cost flexible-budget variance is:
questions.explain: Spending Rs 5,000 less than budget raises operating income, so 5,000 F. Fixed cost has no sales-volume variance because it does not flex with units.

questions.q: Suppose Webb had sold 11,000 jackets with everything else at budget (price Rs 180, variable cost Rs 99, fixed Rs 710,000). What would the sales-volume variance of operating income be against the 12,000-unit static budget? (Unfavourable as a negative number.)
questions.explain: −1,000 × 81 = −81,000 (81,000 U). Flexible-budget operating income would be 11,000 × 81 − 710,000 = Rs 181,000.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Using budgets and variances to judge managers, investigate problems and plan in a garment or textile business.

questions.q: A sales manager at Webb says the 237,000 U variance proves the factory wasted money. What does Level 2 analysis actually show?
options: All 237,000 U is factory inefficiency
162,000 U is due to selling 2,000 fewer jackets, which is a sales problem; 75,000 U is the operating managers' flexible-budget variance
The factory saved money and sales lost it all
Fixed costs were overspent
questions.explain: The sales-volume variance (162,000 U) arises from volume, not factory efficiency; the flexible-budget variance (75,000 U) is what the factory and marketing operations should answer for.

questions.q: Comparing actual variable costs of Rs 1,120,000 directly with the static budget of Rs 1,188,000 shows a 68,000 F variance. Why is this misleading?
options: Because fixed costs are included
Because the static budget is for 12,000 jackets while only 10,000 were made; at 10,000 the budget is Rs 990,000 and costs were really 130,000 U
Because actual costs are always lower
Because revenue was higher
questions.explain: Fewer units should cost less; the flexible budget removes that effect and reveals that each jacket cost Rs 112 instead of Rs 99. This is the central reason for flexible budgets.

questions.q: A favourable price variance on revenue can hide a volume problem: Webb charged Rs 5 more per jacket but sold 2,000 fewer.
questions.explain: Revenue shows 50,000 F at Level 2 but 310,000 U at Level 1; the higher price may even have contributed to the lower volume, which is why the two are analysed separately.

questions.q: Which manager should be asked to explain the 130,000 U variable-cost flexible-budget variance?
options: The managers responsible for production and marketing operations at 10,000 units
The sales manager who set the volume
The owner who approved the static budget
Nobody — it is caused by volume
questions.explain: The flexible-budget variance is measured at the actual output, so it reflects how efficiently resources were used and what prices were paid, not how many jackets were sold.

questions.q: A textile mill prepares only a static budget and compares every month's actual costs with it. Which problem is most likely?
options: Costs will always look unfavourable
In months of low output costs look favourable and in months of high output unfavourable, regardless of efficiency
The budget will be too detailed
Fixed costs will vary with output
questions.explain: Without flexing, volume differences masquerade as cost control. A flexible budget restates the plan for the actual output before judging efficiency.

questions.q: According to the budgeting cycle, what should follow the discovery of a large unfavourable variance?
options: Rewriting last month's budget to match actuals
Investigating the cause, taking corrective action and feeding the lesson into the next plan
Ignoring it if sales were good
Reducing the standard cost
questions.explain: Steps 3 and 4 of the cycle: investigate variations and act, then plan again with the feedback. Changing the past budget defeats the purpose.

questions.q: Webb's fixed costs came in at Rs 705,000 against Rs 710,000. A manager wants a bonus for the 5,000 F. Which caution is most relevant?
options: Fixed cost variances are always unfavourable
Fixed cost should be compared with the flexible budget, which is the same Rs 710,000, so the saving is real but small next to the 130,000 U on variable cost
A saving on fixed cost is impossible
Fixed cost should have fallen by 2,000 ÷ 12,000
questions.explain: The saving is genuine (fixed cost does not flex), but variances must be read together: a Rs 5,000 saving does not offset Rs 130,000 overspent on variable cost.

questions.q: A garment unit's standard variable cost per jacket is Rs 99. Purchasing switches to a cheaper but weaker cloth. Where would you expect the effects to appear?
options: A favourable materials variance and possibly an unfavourable labour variance from rework
Only in the sales-volume variance
Only in fixed costs
Nowhere, because the standard stays Rs 99
questions.explain: Cheaper cloth lowers material spend (F) but weaker cloth can raise labour hours or wastage (U). Variances are signals to investigate, not verdicts on their own.

questions.q: Because the static budget assumed 12,000 jackets, it should be revised to 10,000 after the month to remove the unfavourable variance.
questions.explain: The static budget is not altered; instead a flexible budget is prepared alongside it so that the volume effect is shown separately as the sales-volume variance.

questions.q: A costing office wants a quick test of whether an unfavourable total variance is mainly a sales problem or an operations problem. The best first step is to:
options: Compute the price variance of materials
Prepare the flexible budget at actual output and split the static-budget variance into sales-volume and flexible-budget parts
Compare this month with last month
Recalculate fixed costs
questions.explain: That is Level 2 analysis: the sales-volume variance measures the volume shortfall, the flexible-budget variance measures everything else. Price and efficiency splits come later (lecture 14).

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions that combine the levels of analysis, signs of variances and two-step reasoning.

questions.q: Actual revenue was Rs 1,850,000 on 10,000 jackets. What was the actual average selling price per jacket?
questions.explain: 1,850,000 ÷ 10,000 = Rs 185, Rs 5 above the Rs 180 budget, which explains the 50,000 F revenue flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: Actual variable cost was Rs 1,120,000 for 10,000 jackets. By how many rupees per jacket did actual variable cost exceed the Rs 99 standard?
questions.explain: Actual Rs 112 per jacket − Rs 99 = Rs 13 per jacket; × 10,000 = the 130,000 U flexible-budget variance.

questions.q: A student computes the sales-volume variance of revenue as 360,000 U and reports it as the sales-volume variance of operating income. What is missing?
options: The fixed cost saved
The 198,000 F of variable cost not incurred on the 2,000 unsold jackets, which reduces the net effect to 162,000 U
The price increase of Rs 5
Nothing, 360,000 U is correct
questions.explain: Selling 2,000 fewer jackets loses Rs 360,000 of revenue but saves 2,000 × 99 = Rs 198,000 of variable cost; the net loss of contribution is 2,000 × 81 = Rs 162,000.

questions.q: The flexible-budget variances are: revenue 50,000 F, variable costs 130,000 U, fixed costs 5,000 F. What is the flexible-budget variance of operating income? (Unfavourable as a negative number.)
questions.explain: +50,000 − 130,000 + 5,000 = −75,000, i.e. 75,000 U. Together with 162,000 U sales-volume variance this gives the 237,000 U Level 0 figure.

questions.q: Webb's Level 2 sheet shows the sales-volume variance of variable costs as +198,000 (F). Why is a cost variance favourable when the company did worse than planned?
options: Because variable costs were controlled well
Because 2,000 fewer jackets meant Rs 198,000 of variable cost was not incurred; on its own that increases operating income
Because the sign convention is reversed for costs
It is an error in the sheet
questions.explain: Each line is judged by its effect on operating income. Lower cost from lower volume is F on that line, but the lost revenue (360,000 U) outweighs it, giving 162,000 U overall.

questions.q: Suppose next April Webb budgets 12,000 jackets again and sells 12,500 at the budgeted price of Rs 180, with variable cost at the Rs 99 standard and fixed costs Rs 710,000. What is the sales-volume variance of operating income? (Favourable as a positive number.)
questions.explain: +500 × 81 = 40,500 F. With all prices and costs at standard, this is also the whole static-budget variance.

questions.q: Which combination of signs is consistent with Webb's April results?
options: Revenue flexible-budget variance F, variable-cost flexible-budget variance U, sales-volume variance U
Revenue flexible-budget variance U, variable-cost flexible-budget variance F, sales-volume variance F
All three favourable
Revenue flexible-budget variance F, variable-cost flexible-budget variance F, sales-volume variance U
questions.explain: Price above budget (50,000 F), unit variable cost above budget (130,000 U), and fewer units sold (162,000 U).

questions.q: Webb's actual operating income was Rs 25,000. If variable cost per jacket had been held to the Rs 99 standard with everything else as actual, what would operating income have been?
questions.explain: Removing the 130,000 U variable-cost variance adds Rs 130,000: 25,000 + 130,000 = Rs 155,000. Cross-check: flexible-budget income Rs 100,000 plus the remaining 50,000 F price and 5,000 F fixed-cost variances also gives Rs 155,000.

questions.q: The flexible budget and the static budget show the same fixed cost of Rs 710,000, so their contribution margins differ only because of the quantity of jackets.
questions.explain: Contribution margin = (180 − 99) × units: 972,000 at 12,000 and 810,000 at 10,000; fixed cost does not enter contribution margin at all.

questions.q: A costing office reports: static-budget variance 237,000 U, sales-volume variance 162,000 U, flexible-budget variance 85,000 U. What is wrong?
options: Nothing — the figures are consistent
The two Level 2 parts must add to the Level 0 variance; 162,000 + 85,000 = 247,000, not 237,000, so one figure is misstated
Sales-volume variance cannot be unfavourable
Flexible-budget variance must be larger than sales-volume variance
questions.explain: Static-budget variance = sales-volume variance + flexible-budget variance by construction. The correct flexible-budget variance for Webb is 75,000 U.
